newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols modestly higher as spot edges up.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols modestly higher as spot edges up.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options were modestly firmer as spot continued edging higher in hectic U.S. trading, traders said.
Implied volatility curves remained positively sloped as the actual volatility did not pick up enough to cause a run for shorter maturities, they added.

"The underlying bidding is coming more from dealer positions that still have short vega," Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A., said of short-covering interest in longer maturities. Back-end options have higher vega, the rate of premium movement per change in implied volatility.
The market continued to see good corporate hedging demand in back-month low-delta mark puts and yen puts, a U.S. bank trader in the West Coast added.
"The market (for shorter-dated options) could accelerate if the dollar broke above 120 (yen), but I think 120 is going to be fairly strong resistance for the time being," he noted.
Front end options have steeper time-decay, although they are richer in gamma, which provides quicker premium acceleration and bigger delta swings against spot movements.

A virtually one-way rise in spot dollar/mark lately was not giving enough opportunities for gamma traders to pocket spot gains through delta hedging, while dollar/yen's ascent had been very slow, traders said.
One-month dollar/mark implied volatility rose 0.4 point from late Monday to 11.0/11.2 percent in afternoon U.S. business, while one-year was 0.2 point higher at 11.1/11.3.
One-month dollar/yen was up 0.4 point at 11.7/11.9 percent, while one-year was little changed at 12.0/12.2.
Dollar/mark climbed above 1.88 marks earlier, the highest level in nearly eight years, while dollar/yen pierced 119 yen.

Front-end volatilities were also under pressure in dollar/Swiss franc, which has been lagging dollar/mark. The one-month dollar/Swiss-to-dollar/mark spread was at 0.1/0/3 point, unchanged from Monday but sharply below usual levels.
"With the general trend for a higher dollar, people think they're better off having Deutschemark gamma than Swiss franc gamma," the West Coast trader said.
But Revercomb said this could be an opportunity to buy Swiss volatilities against mark.
"Generally, if you close your eyes and buy it, it tends to move back toward its longer-term mean at around 1.5," he said.
"The caveat to any spread is that we've seen a lot of standard relationships tend to not hold up in this environment over the last two months," he warned, however.
For example, the usually high correlation between spot dollar/mark and the U.S. Treasury note/German bund yield spreads has turned negative, he noted.

"There is a little danger sometimes in looking at these spreads from a strictly historical perspective...in a market that's running away like this," he said. "But this relationship between dollar/Swiss and dollar/mark is probably safer than most."
